title: Zuri and the Missing Sign
markdown:
In the sunny savanna lived Zuri the zebra. Stripes that shone like a rainbow after rain. She loved counting. More than anything she loved counting the striped birds by the Whispering River. She was a little shy. If a bird flew too fast or a sound was too loud, her knees wobbled. She tried to stand very still. Her best friend was Mako, a meerkat whose nose twitched with endless curiosity. Brave, sometimes too brave, leaping before he looked. “Adventure awaits. Let’s go.”

Every day they met by the big baobab. “Ready to count?” Mako chirped, already scanning the riverbank, whole body wiggling. “Ready.” Zuri’s heart hummed quiet joy. They would spend hours tallying the magnificent swoosh-tails with their long stripes, the zig-zag wings that darted like lightning, and the stripe-bellies that gleamed. It was their perfect peaceful routine, a symphony of numbers and feathers, and Zuri kept the tally in her head so she would not lose a bird to a wobble.

Until a grumpy gust blew the peace away. They reached the usual crossing, where the strong wooden bridge stood. The sign that pointed to the best bird meadow was gone. Bare earth. The river ferry, piloted by Gus the goat, was not moving. Gus was stubborn as a rock that would not budge. He folded his hooves and flicked his bristly beard. “No sign, no crossing. That’s the rule.”

A mystery. Zuri felt a prickle. “Where could it have gone?” Mako was already digging near the dock. “Maybe it fell in the river.” Zuri wrung her hooves, imagining it bobbing away. They searched under prickly bushes, behind smooth grey rocks, into hollow logs. No sign. Then Mako spotted sawdust. A faint trail of wood shavings led from the bank toward Gus’s little hut.

They followed the sawdust, Mako darting ahead, Zuri trotting carefully behind. The trail led past Gus’s wobbly fence, which was missing a few planks, and a bucket that smelled of river and old rope. There, propped open against the fence, holding it just so, was the missing bridge sign. Gus, they realized, must have borrowed it. Zuri’s knees started to feel wobbly. She hated bothering people, especially stubborn goats who said no a lot. But Mako nudged her, whiskers tickling her ear. “Go on. Ask him.”

She took a breath. Stripes seemed to stand a little taller. Gus was polishing his ferry with a grubby cloth. “Excuse me, Gus? Is that our bridge sign holding your gate?”

He blinked large dark eyes. “Well, yes. Just the right size. Until I finish fixing my fishing net, it has to stay. Can’t have the gate swinging shut and letting the fish escape.”

A flutter in her tummy. She wanted to hide. Then she remembered the birds she had counted, patterns strong and steady, each stripe in its place. She squared her shoulders. “We need the sign to find the striped birds. Mako and I have a whole club. We haven’t missed a counting day all year.” She looked Gus in his goat eye. Mako watched, silent, supportive.

Gus sighed, dusty air. “Oh, alright.” Softer, like a stream. “Let me finish this knot. Don’t tell anyone I used it as a gate prop. A bit embarrassing.”

He removed the sign, dusty, shavings clinging, intact. The gate swung free with a soft creak. Warm sun on Zuri’s back. Sweet river reeds. Pride, not from being fastest or loudest: from being clear and steady. Gus offered a sheepish apology. The ferry began to chug, cheerful, across the water.

Ever since then Zuri’s knees still wiggled sometimes when a bird flew past too quickly, but she knew she could be brave enough to ask. She and Mako continued their bird-counting adventures, club stronger than ever. On the far bank the striped birds were waiting as if they had been counted in advance. The sign sat back on its post, pointing at the meadow, a little dusty, as if it had only been helping a goat with a gate and a fishing net that still needed one more knot.
